chunks: Typical I2C clock speeds. The question: What are typical clock speeds?
I2C runs at a few standard speeds. The common ones are 100 kilohertz ("Standard"), 400 kilohertz ("Fast") and 1 megahertz ("Fast-mode Plus").
The number is how many clock ticks per second the bus runs, and one bit moves per tick. It is a ceiling, not a promise.
The wire's slow rise, the slowest chip, and the extra bits for addressing and acknowledgments all hold the real data rate lower.
Think of a road with a posted speed limit. The limit is the clock rate. A convoy can only go as fast as its slowest car, so one slow chip slows the whole bus.
Toll booths along the way, such as the address byte and the acknowledgment after each byte, eat time too. So your real average speed ends up below the posted limit.
At 2. 2 kilohms, Standard mode tolerates 536 picofarads (so the 400 picofarads spec ceiling dominates), Fast mode 161 picofarads, and Fm+ about 64 picofarads.
So a 150 picofarads bus is a Fast-mode bus with 2.
2 kilohms; to use 1 megahertz you would need smaller resistors (which the 20 milliamps Fm+ drivers allow) or much less capacitance.
Clock frequency (SCL): ticks per second on the clock wire. One data bit moves each tick. Rise time limit: the longest allowed time for the wire to climb to high.
It is 1000 nanoseconds, 300 nanoseconds and 120 nanoseconds for the three modes above. Bus capacitance: charge the wire and parts soak up, which slows the rise.
ACK: a one-bit "got it" reply that follows every byte. Overhead: bits that carry no data, such as the address, the ACKs, and the start and stop markers.
At 100 kilohertz each tick lasts 10 microseconds. A byte takes 8 data bits plus 1 ACK bit, so 9 ticks, which is 90 microseconds. That is at most about 11,000 bytes per second.
At 400 kilohertz a byte takes 22. 5 microseconds, about 44,000 bytes per second. That is the whole idea.
"The standard speeds are 100 kilohertz Standard, 400 kilohertz Fast, 1 megahertz Fast-mode Plus, and 3. 4 megahertz High-speed, plus a 5 megahertz write-only Ultra-fast mode.
Most sensors run at 100 or 400 kilohertz.
Those are ceilings set by rise time, since the pull-up has to charge the bus capacitance within 1 microseconds, 300 nanoseconds or 120 nanoseconds, and by the slowest device.
Each byte costs nine clocks, so 400 kilohertz is at most about 44 kilobytes per second."
